requirements: Reproduce the paper 'Why DPO is a Misspecified Estimator and How to Fix It' from scratch.

sub_tasks.requirements: The mathematical machinery defined in Section 2, Section 3.1 and Section 4.1 that the paper's experiments and analysis depend on has been implemented: the BTL preference model, the parametric policy class and its implicit reward, the KL-regularized RLHF objective, the empirical and population DPO losses, the weighted KL-projection of Proposition 1, and the local linear/quadratic geometry (Jacobian, Fisher matrix, natural-gradient solution, and reward equivalence classes).
The Bradley-Terry-Luce preference model of Section 2 has been implemented, together with the preference-dataset generating process it induces.

The BTL preference probability p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r*) = sigma(r*(s,a) - r*(s,a')) has been implemented as a function of a latent reward r*: S x A -> R and two responses a, a' at prompt s, where sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z}).

A preference dataset D = {(s^(i), a_w^(i), a_l^(i)) : i in [n]} is generated by drawing the prompt s from the distribution rho over the finite set S and drawing the response pair (a_w, a_l) from the base policy pi_ref(.|s) = pi_{theta_0}(.|s) over the finite set A, as specified in Section 2.

The pairwise count model of Section 2 has been implemented: for each triplet (s, a, a') the number of queries n_{s,a,a'} is fixed in advance and non-random, and the observed win count satisfies N_{s,a_w,a_l} ~ Binomial(n_{s,a_w,a_l}, p^BTL_{s,a_w,a_l}(r*)).

The shift invariance of the BTL model has been verified: adding a constant offset to the latent reward at a given prompt leaves every preference probability sigma(r*(s,a) - r*(s,a')) unchanged, which is the property the paper invokes to replace r* = [2, 3, 1] with the equivalent r* = [1, 2, 0] in Proposition 3.
The parametric policy class of Section 2 and the implicit reward function it induces have been implemented.

A parametric policy pi_theta: S -> Delta(A) smoothly parameterized by theta in R^d has been implemented, supporting the non-tabular regime d << m where m = |S| * |A|, including the neural softmax form pi_theta(a|s) = exp(f_theta(s,a)) / sum_{a'} exp(f_theta(s,a')) given in Section 2.
The tabular special case named in Section 2 is representable: d = m = |S| * |A| with pi_theta(a|s) = theta_{s,a} subject to sum_{s,a} theta_{s,a} = 1.

The implicit reward function r^beta_theta(s,a) = beta * log(pi_theta(a|s) / pi_{theta_0}(a|s)) has been implemented as a function of the policy parameter theta, the fixed base parameter theta_0, and the deviation level beta > 0.
The identity r^beta_{theta_0} == 0 stated in Section 2 holds in the implementation: the implicit reward evaluated at the base parameter theta_0 is identically zero on S x A.

The set R^beta = {r^beta_theta : theta in R^d} of Section 2, the image of the policy parameter space under theta -> r^beta_theta, is represented as a proper subset of R^m for a non-tabular policy class.
The KL-regularized RLHF objective of Section 2 and its tabular closed-form solution have been implemented.

The KL-regularized RLHF objective of Equation 1, J(theta; r*) = E_{rho, pi_theta}[r*(s,a)] - beta * E_{s~rho}[D_KL(pi_theta(.|s) || pi_{theta_0}(.|s))], has been implemented as a function of theta, the latent reward r*, the prompt distribution rho, the base policy pi_{theta_0}, and beta > 0.

The tabular closed-form solution of Equation 2 has been implemented: pi_{theta*}(a|s) = (1/Z*(s)) * pi_{theta_0}(a|s) * exp(r*(s,a)/beta) with partition function Z*(s) = sum_{a in A} pi_{theta_0}(a|s) * exp(r*(s,a)/beta), equivalently r*(s,a) = beta * log(pi_{theta*}(a|s)/pi_{theta_0}(a|s)) + beta * log Z*(s).

The reward-policy reparameterization of Section 2 has been verified: under Equation 2 the BTL preference probability can be written purely in terms of the optimal and base policies as p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r*) = sigma(r^beta_{theta*}(s,a) - r^beta_{theta*}(s,a')), because the partition function beta * log Z*(s) cancels in the difference.
Both the empirical and the population DPO losses of Section 2 have been implemented and can be minimized numerically.
The empirical DPO loss L_D(theta) = -sum_{i=1}^n log sigma(r^beta_theta(s^(i), a_w^(i)) - r^beta_theta(s^(i), a_l^(i))) has been implemented over a finite preference dataset D.

The count-aggregated rewriting of the empirical DPO loss given in Section 2, L_D(theta) = -sum_{s,a_w,a_l} N_{s,a_w,a_l} * log sigma(r^beta_theta(s,a_w) - r^beta_theta(s,a_l)), evaluates to the same value as the per-sample form on the same dataset.

The population DPO loss of Equation 3, L(theta) = -sum_{s,a,a'} n_{s,a,a'} * [p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r*) * log p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r^beta_theta) + (1 - p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r*)) * log(1 - p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r^beta_theta))], has been implemented.

The pairwise query counts n_{s,a,a'} enter the population DPO loss as per-triplet weights that are supplied as an explicit configurable input, so that the count distribution can be varied while the latent reward r*, the base policy and beta are held fixed.
The minimizer theta_DPO of the population DPO loss over theta in R^d is obtained numerically, returning both theta_DPO and its induced implicit reward r^beta_{theta_DPO}.
The weighted KL-projection characterization of DPO given in Proposition 1 has been implemented and checked numerically.
The Kullback-Leibler divergence between two Bernoulli random variables, d_KL(p||q) = p * log(p/q) + (1-p) * log((1-p)/(1-q)), has been implemented as used in Equation 4.

The weighted KL-projection objective of Equation 4, argmin_{r in R^beta} sum_{s,a,a'} n_{s,a,a'} * d_KL(p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r*) || p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r)), has been implemented as an optimization over the implicit reward manifold R^beta with the pairwise counts n_{s,a,a'} as projection weights.

Proposition 1 has been checked numerically on a concrete instance: minimizing the population DPO loss of Equation 3 over theta and solving the weighted KL-projection of Equation 4 over R^beta return the same implicit reward r^beta_{theta_DPO}.

The realizable case discussed immediately after Proposition 1 has been checked numerically: when the latent reward is chosen so that r* = r^beta_theta for some theta, the DPO minimizer recovers that same theta, which coincides with the RLHF-optimal parameter theta*.
The local linearization of the implicit reward manifold developed in Section 3.1 has been implemented.
The d x m Jacobian matrix A_{theta_0} has been constructed with the score vector grad log pi_{theta_0}(a|s) placed in its (s,a)-th column, evaluated at the base parameter theta_0.

The first-order Taylor expansion of the implicit reward around theta_0 given in Section 3.1 has been implemented as r^beta_theta ~= beta * A_{theta_0}^T * (theta - theta_0), equivalently beta * grad log pi_{theta_0}(a|s)^T (theta - theta_0) for each (s,a).

The linear manifold approximation R^beta ~= C(A_{theta_0}^T) of Section 3.1 has been implemented: the set of linearized implicit rewards is the column space of A_{theta_0}^T, a subspace of R^m of dimension at most d.

It has been verified that the linear manifold approximation C(A_{theta_0}^T) does not depend on beta and is a function only of the policy class and the base policy pi_{theta_0}, as stated at the end of the derivation in Section 3.1.

The claim of Remark 2 and Proposition 8(iii) has been checked numerically: the discrepancy |r^beta_theta(s,a) - beta * grad log pi_{theta_0}(a|s)^T (theta - theta_0)| over a bounded neighborhood of theta_0 falls below any prescribed tolerance epsilon once beta exceeds a sufficiently large beta_min.
The local quadratic approximation of the RLHF objective and the resulting natural-gradient characterization of theta* from Section 4.1 have been implemented.
The m x m diagonal matrix D_{rho,theta_0} carrying the scaled base-policy probabilities rho(s) * pi_{theta_0}(a|s) on its diagonal has been implemented.
The d x m matrix A_{rho,theta_0} = A_{theta_0} * D_{rho,theta_0}, whose columns hold the scaled gradients rho(s) * grad pi_{theta_0}(a|s), has been implemented.
The d x d Fisher information matrix F_{rho,theta_0} = E_{rho, pi_{theta_0}}[grad log pi_{theta_0}(a|s) grad log pi_{theta_0}(a|s)^T] at the base policy has been implemented.

The first-order Taylor approximation of the expected reward given in Section 4.1, E_{rho,pi_theta}[r*(s,a)] ~= E_{rho,pi_{theta_0}}[r*(s,a)] + (theta - theta_0)^T A_{rho,theta_0} r*, has been implemented.
The second-order Taylor approximation of the KL penalty given in Section 4.1, D_KL(pi_theta || pi_{theta_0}) ~= (1/2) (theta - theta_0)^T F_{rho,theta_0} (theta - theta_0), has been implemented.

The combined local quadratic approximation of the RLHF objective from Section 4.1, J(theta; r*) ~= E_{rho,pi_{theta_0}}[r*(s,a)] + (theta - theta_0)^T A_{rho,theta_0} r* - (beta/2) (theta - theta_0)^T F_{rho,theta_0} (theta - theta_0), has been implemented.
The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse F^dagger_{rho,theta_0} of the (possibly rank-deficient) Fisher information matrix has been computed, as required by the closed form in Equation 5.

The relation of Equation 5 has been implemented: A_{rho,theta_0} r* = beta * F_{rho,theta_0} (theta* - theta_0), solved as theta* = theta_0 + (1/beta) * F^dagger_{rho,theta_0} * A_{rho,theta_0} r*, which the paper identifies as a natural policy gradient step (Kakade, 2001).

The claim of Remark 5 and Proposition 8(iv) has been checked numerically: over a bounded neighborhood of theta_0, the gap between the exact objective J(theta; r*) of Equation 1 and its local quadratic approximation falls below any prescribed tolerance epsilon once beta exceeds a sufficiently large beta_min.
The RLHF-induced reward equivalence classes of Section 4.1, and their relationship to DPO's linearized implicit rewards, have been implemented and checked.

The equivalence class of Equation 6, R^beta_eq(theta) = {r in R^m : A_{rho,theta_0} r = beta * F_{rho,theta_0} (theta - theta_0)}, has been implemented as an affine subspace of R^m whose membership can be tested for a given reward vector.
A basis for the null space N(A_{rho,theta_0}) = {delta in R^m : A_{rho,theta_0} delta = 0} has been computed, for example via SVD or another rank-revealing decomposition.
Lemma 6 has been checked numerically: for a fixed theta, two reward vectors r_1 and r_2 both lie in R^beta_eq(theta) exactly when their difference r_1 - r_2 lies in N(A_{rho,theta_0}).

Proposition 7 has been checked numerically: the element of R^beta_eq(theta) minimizing the Mahalanobis norm ||r||_{D_{rho,theta_0}} = sqrt(r^T D_{rho,theta_0} r) equals the DPO linearization r^beta_theta = beta * A_{theta_0}^T (theta - theta_0).

The bijective correspondence asserted in Proposition 7 has been checked: distinct policy parameters theta yield distinct equivalence classes R^beta_eq(theta), each represented by its own linearized implicit reward r^beta_theta.

The observation following Lemma 6 has been checked: for the tabular policy class the equivalence class R^beta_eq(theta) collapses to the DPO implicit reward r^beta_theta(s,a) = beta * log(pi_theta(a|s)/pi_{theta_0}(a|s)), up to the prompt-dependent shift beta * log Z_theta(s) noted in the paper's footnote.

The didactic single-prompt, three-response bandit instance of Proposition 3 has been reproduced, exhibiting DPO's preference reversal, likelihood displacement, expected-reward reduction and sensitivity to the pairwise count distribution, together with the geometric picture of Figure 2.
The bandit instance specified in the proof of Proposition 3 has been constructed.
A promptless (single-prompt) problem with exactly three responses a_1, a_2, a_3 has been constructed, so that |A| = 3 and m = 3, as specified in Proposition 3.
The latent reward vector r* = [2, 3, 1] over the responses (a_1, a_2, a_3) stated in the proof of Proposition 3 has been set.
The BTL-equivalent reward r* = [1, 2, 0] used in the paper's derivation has been substituted for [2, 3, 1], on the grounds that both induce the same preference distribution.
The induced true preference order a_2 > a_1 > a_3 has been computed from r* under the BTL model, identifying a_2 as the highest-reward response and a_1 as the second-highest.
The one-dimensional linear softmax policy class of Proposition 3, pi_theta = (1/Z) * [e^theta, e^{-theta}, 1] with Z = 1 + e^theta + e^{-theta} and theta in R (d = 1), has been implemented.
The base policy has been set to theta_0 = 0, giving the uniform base policy pi_{theta_0} = [1/3, 1/3, 1/3] as specified in Proposition 3.
The base-policy expected reward has been computed as pi_{theta_0}^T r* = (1/3)(1 + 2 + 0) = 1 under r* = [1, 2, 0], the baseline against which failure mode (iii) of Proposition 3 is judged.

The experiment is run in the large-beta regime beta >> 1 required by Proposition 3, so that the local linear approximation of R^beta is accurate and the observed failure modes are attributable to misspecified geometry rather than to linearization error.
The local geometry of the bandit instance has been computed and shown to place the latent reward off the implicit reward manifold.

The policy gradient matrix at general theta given in Proposition 3, A_theta = (1/Z) * [1 + 2e^{-theta}, -(1 + 2e^theta), e^{-theta} - e^theta], has been implemented for the one-dimensional softmax policy class.
Evaluating the policy gradient matrix at theta_0 = 0 yields A_{theta_0} = [1, -1, 0], as stated in the proof of Proposition 3.

The local linear approximation of the implicit reward manifold has been computed as R^beta ~= span([1, -1, 0]) in R^3, so every implicit reward DPO can express in the neighborhood of theta_0 has the form [alpha, -alpha, 0].

It has been verified that the latent reward r* = [1, 2, 0] does not lie in span([1, -1, 0]), so this instance is misspecified in the sense of Proposition 1 and the projection of Equation 4 is non-trivial.
The imbalanced pairwise count regime of Proposition 3 has been configured and the resulting DPO solution computed.

The pairwise query counts have been set to satisfy the condition of Proposition 3, n_{3,1} >> max{n_{1,2}, n_{2,3}}, so that comparisons between a_1 and a_3 dominate the population DPO loss; the paper prescribes only this dominance relation and not specific count values, so any counts realizing it are acceptable.
The population DPO loss of Equation 3 has been minimized over the scalar parameter theta for the bandit instance under the imbalanced counts, producing theta_DPO.

The mechanism described in the proof of Proposition 3 has been confirmed: because n_{3,1} dominates, the projection drives p^BTL_{1,3}(r^beta_theta) close to p^BTL_{1,3}(r*), which forces the reward gap r^beta_theta(a_1) - r^beta_theta(a_3) to be of order alpha for some alpha > 0.

The DPO solution under the imbalanced counts has been computed and agrees with the paper's r^beta_theta ~= [alpha, -alpha, 0] with alpha > 0, i.e. it is the point of span([1, -1, 0]) with a positive first coordinate.
The recovered policy parameter satisfies theta_DPO = O(alpha) > 0, the sign stated in the proof of Proposition 3 for the imbalanced regime.
Failure mode (i) of Proposition 3, preference reversal, has been demonstrated.
The DPO-learned implicit reward assigns r^beta_theta(a_1) = alpha > 0 > -alpha = r^beta_theta(a_2), ranking a_1 above a_2 and thereby reversing the true order a_2 > a_1 induced by r* = [1, 2, 0].

Failure mode (i) has been verified at the policy level: the DPO policy satisfies pi_theta(a_1) > pi_theta(a_2), so it favors the response with the second-highest true reward over the response with the highest true reward.
Failure mode (ii) of Proposition 3, movement of the response probabilities in the wrong direction relative to the base policy, has been demonstrated.
The DPO policy satisfies pi_theta(a_2) < pi_{theta_0}(a_2) = 1/3: the probability of the highest-reward response decreases relative to the base policy.
The DPO policy satisfies pi_theta(a_1) > pi_{theta_0}(a_1) = 1/3: the probability of the second-highest-reward response increases relative to the base policy.

The measured probability changes show pi_theta(a_1) and pi_theta(a_2) moving in opposite directions, which aspect 1 of the discussion following Proposition 3 identifies as strictly more extreme than the likelihood displacement of Razin et al. (2024) and Pal et al. (2024), where both probabilities move together while their difference is presumed to grow.
Failure mode (iii) of Proposition 3, a decrease in expected reward relative to the base policy, has been demonstrated.
The expected reward of the DPO policy has been computed in the closed form given in the proof of Proposition 3, pi_theta^T r* = (e^alpha + 2 e^{-alpha}) / (1 + e^alpha + e^{-alpha}).
The strict inequality pi_theta^T r* < 1 = pi_{theta_0}^T r* has been verified, confirming that DPO returns a policy with strictly lower expected reward than the base policy under the true reward.

The expected reward of the RLHF-optimal policy obtained from Equation 5 on this same instance is at least the base-policy value of 1, contrasting with DPO's decrease and matching aspect 2 of the discussion following Proposition 3, which notes that two-stage RLHF cannot decrease expected reward on any policy class when the reward is learned accurately.
The sensitivity of the DPO solution to the pairwise count distribution described in aspect 5 of the discussion following Proposition 3 has been demonstrated.

A second count regime has been configured in which the a_1-versus-a_2 comparisons dominate, n_{1,2} >> {n_{2,3}, n_{3,1}}, with the latent reward, policy class, base policy and beta held identical to the imbalanced run.
Under the n_{1,2}-dominant counts, DPO learns the desired reward function r^beta_theta ~= [-alpha, alpha, 0] with alpha > 0, correctly ranking a_2 above a_1.
The policy parameter recovered under the n_{1,2}-dominant counts is negative, theta < 0, the sign opposite to the imbalanced regime.
Under the n_{1,2}-dominant counts the learned policy satisfies pi_theta(a_2) > pi_theta(a_1), so the preference reversal of failure mode (i) is absent.

Under the n_{1,2}-dominant counts the learned policy satisfies pi_theta(a_2) > pi_{theta_0}(a_2) = 1/3, so the probability of the highest-reward response increases rather than decreases relative to the base policy.
Under the n_{1,2}-dominant counts the expected reward pi_theta^T r* does not fall below the base-policy value of 1, so the reward reduction of failure mode (iii) is absent.

A count regime under which the DPO minimizer stays at or near the base policy has been identified, completing the three qualitative outcomes aspect 5 of the discussion following Proposition 3 attributes to varying {n_{i,j}}: the desired result, the opposite one, or no movement at all.

The two count regimes are reported side by side, showing that changing only the relative proportions of {n_{i,j}} flips the sign of theta_DPO and reverses which response the learned reward prefers, which the paper identifies as itself a failure mode of DPO.
The two modelling assumptions the paper uses to rule out competing explanations for the failure modes have been honoured in the reproduction.

The failure modes are demonstrated on the population DPO loss rather than on a finite sample, so that they arise with unlimited clean preference data generated by the BTL model and cannot be attributed to scarce-data sampling effects, as argued in aspect 3 of the discussion following Proposition 3.

The DPO loss is solved to (near) optimality rather than by a fixed number of gradient steps, so that the demonstrated failure modes are properties of the loss minimizer and not of any particular optimization algorithm, as argued in aspect 4 of the discussion following Proposition 3.
Remark 4, which shows that global coverage is not sufficient for DPO optimality, has been reproduced on the bandit instance.

The global coverage constant of the bandit instance has been computed as max_{s,a} pi_theta(a|s) / pi_{theta_0}(a|s) <= C with C = 3 for all theta in R, confirming the value stated in Remark 4 for the uniform base policy.

It has been reported that the bandit instance satisfies the global coverage condition of Song et al. (2024) with C = 3 and nevertheless exhibits the Proposition 3 failure modes, establishing that global coverage is necessary but not sufficient for DPO to reach the optimal policy.
Figure 2, the geometric picture of the bandit instance, has been reproduced.

The set of implicit rewards DPO can project onto in the bandit instance, shown as the shaded region in Figure 2, has been traced by sweeping the relative proportions of the pairwise counts n_{1,2}, n_{2,3}, n_{3,1} and recording the resulting minimizers r^beta_theta.

A plot in the (r_1, r_2) plane matching Figure 2 has been produced, showing the line C(A_{theta_0}^T) = span([1, -1, 0]), the latent reward r* = [1, 2, 0], the base implicit reward r^beta_{theta_0} at the origin, the achievable projection region, and the located solution r^beta_theta in the theta > 0 half of the line.
AuxDPO, the paper's proposed direct alignment algorithm, has been implemented in both its population form (Equation 7) and its empirical form, and validated on the didactic bandit instance.
The nullspace argument of Section 4.2 that motivates the auxiliary variables has been implemented.

The decomposition r* = r^beta_{theta*} + delta with delta in N(A_{rho,theta_0}) has been implemented, following from Lemma 6 and the fact that r* and r^beta_{theta*} lie in the same RLHF equivalence class.

The rank-nullity argument of Section 4.2 has been verified: jointly varying theta in R^d and delta in N(A_{rho,theta_0}) reaches the whole reward space R^m, whereas DPO searches only C(A_{theta_0}^T), a subspace of dimension at most d.
The population AuxDPO objective of Equation 7 has been implemented.
The augmented implicit reward r^beta_{theta,delta} used in Equation 7, which adds the auxiliary variable delta to the policy-induced implicit reward r^beta_theta, has been implemented.

The population AuxDPO objective of Equation 7 has been implemented as the minimization of L(theta, delta) = -sum_{s,a,a'} n_{s,a,a'} [p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r*) log p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r^beta_{theta,delta}) + (1 - p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r*)) log(1 - p^BTL_{s,a,a'}(r^beta_{theta,delta}))] jointly over theta in R^d and delta in N(A_{rho,theta_0}).

Proposition 9 has been checked numerically: for sufficiently large beta the minimizer of Equation 7 attains theta = theta* up to an O(epsilon) error, in contrast to the DPO minimizer on the same instance.
The empirical AuxDPO loss of Section 4.2, which is the form actually trainable on a finite preference dataset, has been implemented.

The auxiliary variable vector delta = {delta(s^(i), a_w^(i)), delta(s^(i), a_l^(i))}_{i=1}^n in R^{2n} has been introduced as trainable parameters separate from theta, carrying exactly one scalar per response in each of the n preference pairs.

The log-sigmoid term of the empirical AuxDPO loss has been implemented as -(1/n) sum_{i=1}^n log sigma(r^beta_theta(s^(i), a_w^(i)) - r^beta_theta(s^(i), a_l^(i)) + delta(s^(i), a_w^(i)) - delta(s^(i), a_l^(i))), with the auxiliary variables entering additively inside the sigmoid.

The nullspace penalty term has been implemented as lambda * || (1/(2n)) sum_{i=1}^n (delta(s^(i), a_w^(i)) grad log pi_{theta_0}(a_w^(i)|s^(i)) + delta(s^(i), a_l^(i)) grad log pi_{theta_0}(a_l^(i)|s^(i))) ||_2^2 and added to the log-sigmoid term.

The penalty has been implemented as the squared norm of a Monte-Carlo estimate of A_{rho,theta_0} delta, using the identity A_{rho,theta_0} delta = E_{rho, pi_{theta_0}}[delta(s,a) grad log pi_{theta_0}(a|s)] stated in Section 4.2.
The score vectors grad log pi_{theta_0}(a|s) appearing in the penalty are taken from the frozen base policy pi_{theta_0} rather than from the policy being trained.
The constrained optimization over delta in N(A_{rho,theta_0}) subset R^m has been converted into an unconstrained optimization over R^{2n} by adding the penalty term, as described in Section 4.2.
The penalty coefficient lambda > 0 is exposed as a configurable hyperparameter controlling how strongly the nullspace constraint is enforced.
The empirical AuxDPO loss is minimized jointly over the policy parameters theta and the auxiliary variables delta, with both receiving gradient updates during training.
The total trainable parameter count has been verified to be d + 2n = O(d), reflecting the paper's observation that typically n << d and 2n << m, so the auxiliary variables add negligible overhead.
AuxDPO has been validated on the didactic bandit instance of Proposition 3, where DPO fails.

AuxDPO has been run on the three-response bandit instance under the same imbalanced counts n_{3,1} >> max{n_{1,2}, n_{2,3}} that cause DPO to fail, with r*, the policy class, the base policy and beta held identical to the DPO run.

AuxDPO recovers a policy parameter agreeing with the RLHF-optimal theta* obtained from Equation 5, which for this instance evaluates to theta* = theta_0 + (1/beta) F^dagger_{rho,theta_0} A_{rho,theta_0} r* = -1/(2 beta) using F_{rho,theta_0} = 2/3 and A_{rho,theta_0} r* = -1/3; in particular the recovered parameter is negative, the sign opposite to theta_DPO.

The recovered auxiliary variable accounts for the off-manifold component of the latent reward, delta = r* - r^beta_{theta*} = [1, 2, 0] - [-1/2, 1/2, 0] = [3/2, 3/2, 0], and satisfies A_{rho,theta_0} delta = 0, i.e. it lies in N(A_{rho,theta_0}).
The AuxDPO policy on the bandit instance satisfies pi_theta(a_2) > pi_theta(a_1), avoiding the preference reversal that DPO exhibits under the same counts.
The AuxDPO policy on the bandit instance satisfies pi_theta(a_2) > pi_{theta_0}(a_2) = 1/3, avoiding the decrease in the highest-reward response's probability that DPO exhibits.
The expected reward of the AuxDPO policy on the bandit instance is not below the base-policy value of 1, avoiding the reward reduction that DPO exhibits under the same counts.
AuxDPO has been reported to outperform DPO on the didactic bandit setting, supporting the abstract's claim of superior performance on didactic bandit settings.
Figure 3, the geometric picture of how AuxDPO repairs the misspecification, has been reproduced.

A plot in the (r_1, r_2) plane matching Figure 3 has been produced, showing the line C(A_{theta_0}^T), the shaded set of reachable DPO projections, the equivalence classes R^beta_eq(theta) and R^beta_eq(theta*) as parallel affine lines, the direction delta in N(A_{rho,theta_0}) along which AuxDPO's auxiliary variables move, the latent reward r*, and the resulting point r^beta_{theta,delta}.

It has been verified that in the reproduced figure the latent reward r* lies on the equivalence class R^beta_eq(theta*), whose minimum-Mahalanobis-norm representative r^beta_{theta*} is the point at which that class meets the line C(A_{theta_0}^T).

The LLM alignment experiments of Section 5 have been reproduced: AuxDPO is compared against DPO, IPO and DPOP on MMLU-PRO and REWARDBENCH V2 across Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.2-1B and Qwen3-0.6B under both in-domain and out-of-domain protocols, and the numbers of Table 1 and Table 2 are reproduced.
The three datasets named in Section 5 have been acquired and prepared.
The ULTRAFEEDBACK dataset (Cui et al., 2024) has been acquired in the pre-processed and binarized version of Dong et al. (2024), which Section 5 identifies as the training dataset.
The cleaned ULTRAFEEDBACK preference set used for out-of-domain training in Section 5 has been prepared from the binarized dataset.
The REWARDBENCH V2 dataset (Malik et al., 2025) has been acquired as an evaluation dataset.
The acquired REWARDBENCH V2 split contains the 1.87K prompts stated in Section 5.
The REWARDBENCH V2 prompts carry the category structure described in Section 5, covering categories such as factuality, precise instruction following, and focus.
REWARDBENCH V2 is consumed with its chosen and rejected responses used directly, with no conversion step, as Section 5 specifies.

The MMLU-PRO dataset (Wang et al., 2024b) has been acquired as the second evaluation dataset, comprising the 12K multi-discipline questions with ten answer options and one correct answer each described in Section 5.
In converting MMLU-PRO into a preference dataset, the correct answer of each question is filtered out and used as the chosen response a_w, as described in Section 5.
In converting MMLU-PRO into a preference dataset, an incorrect option of each question is used as the rejected response a_l, as described in Section 5.
The three base policies used in Section 5 have been acquired.
The Llama3.1-8B model has been acquired and can be loaded for fine-tuning.
The Llama3.2-1B model has been acquired and can be loaded for fine-tuning.
The Qwen3-0.6B model has been acquired and can be loaded for fine-tuning.

The reference policy pi_{theta_0} used in the implicit reward beta * log(pi_theta(a|s) / pi_{theta_0}(a|s)) is a frozen copy of the base model whose log-probabilities are not updated during fine-tuning.
The in-domain and out-of-domain protocols and the fine-tuning regime of Section 5 have been implemented.

The in-domain protocol has been implemented: each evaluation dataset is split 80/20 into training and evaluation subsets, giving IID comparisons, with models trained on the 80% split and evaluated on the 20% split.
The out-of-domain protocol has been implemented: models are trained on cleaned ULTRAFEEDBACK and evaluated on the preference datasets, with no training data drawn from the evaluation datasets.
All runs are full fine-tuning of the base models, matching Section 5's statement that full fine-tuning results are reported; parameter-efficient alternatives such as LoRA are not substituted.
The KL deviation parameter beta used by every preference optimization method in the LLM runs is exposed as a configurable hyperparameter and the value used is logged.
The three baseline preference optimization methods compared against AuxDPO in Section 5 have been implemented.
The DPO baseline of Rafailov et al. (2023) has been implemented for LLM fine-tuning using the empirical DPO loss over the implicit reward beta * log(pi_theta(a|s) / pi_{theta_0}(a|s)).
The IPO baseline of Azar et al. (2023) has been implemented for LLM fine-tuning.
The DPOP baseline of Pal et al. (2024) has been implemented for LLM fine-tuning.
The fine-tuning runs behind Table 1 and Table 2 have been executed.
All four methods (DPO, AuxDPO, IPO, DPOP) have been fine-tuned on Llama3.1-8B under both the ID and the OOD protocols for both MMLU-PRO and REWARDBENCH V2.
All four methods (DPO, AuxDPO, IPO, DPOP) have been fine-tuned on Llama3.2-1B under both the ID and the OOD protocols for both MMLU-PRO and REWARDBENCH V2.
All four methods (DPO, AuxDPO, IPO, DPOP) have been fine-tuned on Qwen3-0.6B under both the ID and the OOD protocols for both MMLU-PRO and REWARDBENCH V2.
The two distinct accuracy metrics used in Section 5 have been implemented and kept separate.
The Table 1 metric has been implemented: accuracy is the fraction of evaluation prompts for which the fine-tuned model's logits for the chosen response exceed its logits for the rejected response.
Table 1 values are computed as the percentage change in mean accuracy relative to the base policy rather than as raw accuracies, matching the Table 1 caption.
The Table 2 metric has been implemented: accuracy is measured by comparing the fine-tuned model's generated answer against the correct answer provided in the MMLU-PRO dataset.
Evaluation results on MMLU-PRO are aggregated per subject as well as overall, so that the subject-wise breakdown of Table 2 can be produced.
The evaluation harness has been run over every trained checkpoint, producing the accuracy numbers needed to populate Table 1 and Table 2.
